newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens hires Morgan Stanley to sell defense electronics unit.
newsitem.headline: Siemens hires Morgan Stanley to sell defense electronics unit.

text.p: Siemens AG said Tuesday it hired U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley & Co. to sell its defence electronics unit in an effort to focus on its profitable businesses.

The German industrial conglomerate also said its transportation systems unit, VT, will report a larger-than-expected loss of as much as 100 million marks ($57 million) for the current fiscal year. The unit will cut about 800 jobs in Germany and hire outside firms to run some of its operations.

Siemens has been under pressure from investors since November, when it warned that it would not report a profit this fiscal year, which ends Sept. 30. In January the company said it plans to sell off various businesses with total revenue of about 3 billion marks ($1.7 billion).
"I do sense a bit of acceleration, a slight hastening of the process," said Peter Roe, a Banque Paribas analyst in London. "These things they are doing should be well-received by the markets."
Siemens said Morgan Stanley will seek to sell or find a joint-venture partner for its defence electronics business. Siemens did not specify how much it seeks.

The transportation unit, which makes subway trains and locomotives, also increased its loss forecast for the year to about double what analysts had expected. VT previously had said it expected a loss of 80 million marks ($46 million), due to a 68 million mark ($39 million) restructuring charge and more than 100 million marks ($57 million) in costs related to outstanding orders.
"They had some bad orders but seemed to be working through them, so this is disappointing," Roe said.

To boost profit, the unit plans to sell production of overhead lines and power supplies to a group of managers. It also plans to transfer another operation to Siemens' power transmission unit and to cut its headquarter staff by 30 percent.

The unit also will cooperate with competitors to break into new markets, unit head Wolfram Martinsen told a news conference in Vienna. Siemens plans to market rail systems with General Motors Corp.'s locomotive unit and to build mass transit systems in two Chinese cities with ADtranz, he said. With France's GEC Alsthom, the unit would market high-speed train technology.
"We are making the tough decisions in order to thrive in the future," Martinsen said.

"This is a super-competitive industry and there's not a lot of growth," said one Frankfurt analyst who did not want to be identified. "Europe has done a lot of modernising, and in Eastern Europe financing is a question for big projects."
